opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, when I went to Berkeley I wasn't fully committed to AI yet. My background was in theoretical physics, and the postdoc was still very much a physics position. But by then I was already feeling some tension. I loved the field, but in a lot of the areas I worked on, progress had become very slow. You could spend years on a problem, and even if you made headway, it was unclear how much it would change our understanding.

At the same time, AI was clearly going through something dramatic. Large language models were scaling up, and you could see capabilities appearing that nobody had predicted very well. To someone trained in physics, that felt like a new kind of phenomenon: a complex system with emergent behavior that we didn't have a good theory for. That was exciting to me.

So I thought of Berkeley partly as a transition period. It gave me some space. I could keep doing physics while reading a lot, talking to people in AI, and figuring out whether this was a real calling or just a passing curiosity. Berkeley is also a good environment for that. There are a lot of strong people in AI around, and the Bay Area makes it easy to see what's happening in industry.

I think what eventually convinced me was a sense of timing. In physics, if you wait five years, the field will mostly still be where it is. In AI, five years felt like an eternity. If I believed this was one of the most important things happening, then the cost of waiting was very high. So the decision became less about whether I should switch and more about when, and I decided earlier was better than later.

r001.rationale: He describes Berkeley as a transition period that gave him space to continue physics while deciding whether AI was a lasting calling, communicating accommodation for his uncertainty.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it was a bit of a transition period for me, and I didn't treat the two things as mutually exclusive at the time.

When I finished my PhD at Stanford, I was still very much a physicist. The Berkeley position was a very good opportunity — a lot of freedom, no teaching obligations, great people around in condensed matter theory. So the default path was clear: go do a postdoc, keep working on the problems I was already working on, and see where it leads. That's the normal trajectory, and I didn't want to throw it away impulsively.

But at the same time, I had already been paying attention to what was happening in AI for a while. Around 2022, 2023, you could see the capability jumps happening very quickly, and as a physicist you're trained to notice when a field is in a phase where the fundamentals are shifting. I remember thinking, this is probably the most important technology being built in my lifetime, and the question is whether I want to watch it from the outside or be inside it.

So my way of thinking about Berkeley was: this is a place where I can keep doing serious physics, but it's also in the Bay Area, I'm close to the labs, I can talk to people, I can try things, and I can figure out whether my intuitions actually transfer. I treated it partly as a buffer, a place to make the decision carefully instead of making it from a distance. The physics problems I was working on also had a flavor — many-body systems, emergent behavior from simple rules — that made me curious about neural networks as physical objects. So it didn't feel like abandoning one thing for another. It felt more like extending the same curiosity to a new system.

And then in practice, once I actually spent time on it, the pull became pretty strong, and the decision kind of made itself. But I'm glad I went through Berkeley first rather than jumping directly. It gave me a few more years of training in how to think about hard problems carefully, and that turned out to be useful.

r001.rationale: He describes Berkeley as offering freedom to continue physics while exploring AI, and as a buffer to make the decision carefully. This communicates that Berkeley accommodated his uncertainty.

astra-6.text: I think I saw Berkeley as a place to explore what working on AI could actually mean. Being interested in AI is one thing, but knowing which questions you want to spend your time on is another. I didn’t have a very specific research agenda in mind. I wanted to build a strong foundation, get exposed to different ideas, and gradually figure out where I could contribute. So it was less about having a complete plan and more about finding an environment where I could develop one.

r001.rationale: The response says Berkeley offered room to explore and develop a research direction, but does not say Yao reconsidered starting there because Berkeley was willing to accommodate his uncertain plans.

sol-6.1.text: I think, at that point, “going into AI” was still a pretty broad idea for me. I was interested in it, but I didn’t have a clear picture of which problems I wanted to work on, or what doing research would actually feel like. So I thought about Berkeley as a place to explore—to learn the foundations, talk to people, and get a better sense of what interested me. It was less about committing to a very specific path and more about finding an environment where I could figure that path out.

r001.rationale: The response says Yao saw Berkeley as a place to explore while he clarified his interests, but it does not attribute his reconsideration to Berkeley accommodating his uncertain plans.
